After warning Wednesday night about hedges being lifted following the election, Tier1Alpha sees a scramble back into protection with the largest SPX put volume on record:

"Wednesday’s massive hedge unwind likely left many investors considerably offside heading into the decline, triggering an aggressive bid for downside protection. Notably, SPX put volume reached its highest daily level on record, accompanied by a sharp increase in put/call skew and a jump of more than 5 vol points in fixed-strike volatility. Together, these reflected substantial demand for protection even as hedging costs became progressively more expensive throughout the selloff.

"On the dealer side, this created the opposite of Wednesday’s setup, as renewed demand for protective puts left market makers with additional positive delta exposure that then needed to be offset by shorting futures, adding yet another source of selling pressure to an already vulnerable market."

Wall Street’s “fear gauges” just had their biggest day in years. So what normally happens next?

The VIX jumped 69.7% to 28.17 Thursday, its biggest one-day gain since December 2024 and second-largest since the February 2018 “Volmageddon,” per Cboe. It was also its highest close since March 30.

The VVIX (the VIX of the VIX) rose 49.3% to 134.99, its biggest one-day gain since February 2007 and its biggest point gain since Volmageddon. So traders weren’t just hedging against further stock declines, they were scrambling to hedge volatility itself.

What history says (calculations from Cboe data):
▪️ VIX up 60%+ in a day (5 prior cases since 1990): S&P 500 higher a month later all 5 times
▪️ VIX up 40%+ (24 cases): higher a month later 18 times, and a year later 22 times, by an average of almost 19%
▪️ VIX up 40%+ and VVIX up 30%+ the same day (6 cases since 2007): higher a month later every time, but a year later only 4 of 6, averaging about 4%

Big caveat with the small sample sizes, and note it can be just the start of something much bigger, like February 2020, when the S&P was down 24% a month later. 

Getting more granular, spikes from a calm base like this one have had weaker three-month follow-through. And the closest match for both gauges, February 27, 2007, saw the S&P slightly lower a year later.

In Fed speakers, New York Fed President Williams (voter) joins the ECB’s Lane for a moderated discussion in Frankfurt at 4:30am ET, St. Louis Fed President Musalem (non-voter) speaks at a Greater St. Louis Inc. event at 9:10am ET, and Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman discusses supervision and regulation at the University of Mississippi at 12:15pm ET.

There are no non-Bill (>1yr in maturity) US Treasury auctions.

Also, the Justice Department and lawyers for Fed Governor Lisa Cook are due to file a report with a federal judge on how to proceed with her lawsuit challenging President Trump’s attempt to remove her, per Bloomberg (via Barraud).

Six S&P 500 components report, none with market caps over $100B:

Before the open: Moderna (MRNA), Humana (HUM), Vistra (VST), Charter Communications (CHTR) and Franklin Resources (BEN)

Time not announced: PPL (PPL)

Ex-US highlights include Japan September labor cash earnings, Germany September industrial production, France’s September current account and trade balances and Q3 wages, Eurozone September retail sales and Canada’s October Labour Force Survey. The BoE’s Huw Pill also gives a briefing the day after the bank’s decision, and Greece and Israel face credit rating reviews.

tweets.text:
Ahead of today's employment report, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan interestingly all land on the same number for October payrolls: 75,000. That’s above the 65,000 Bloomberg consensus and up from September’s 29,000.

The case for a beat is mostly the lack of layoffs. Goldman notes jobless claims averaged 198,000 in the October survey month. Since then, claims have dropped to 189,000, back to the joint-lowest since 1969, Challenger job cuts were the fewest for any October since 2023, and ADP came in at 86,000.

Where the banks split:

▪️ Unemployment rate: JPMorgan sees 4.1%, while Bank of America and Goldman see 4.2%, although Goldman calling the risks skewed lower. September was 4.175% unrounded, so it doesn’t take much to tip it.
▪️ Hourly earnings: Bank of America and Goldman see 0.3%. JPMorgan sees 0.2%, which would drop the annual pace to 2.8%, a new cycle low.
▪️ Participation: Bank of America sees it falling to 61.7%, JPMorgan rising to 61.9%.
▪️ Seasonals: Goldman says a late Labor Day sets up an October rebound, while Bank of America says October seasonals usually work against payrolls.

Bank of America also flags slowing weekly ADP data (about 17,000 a week in October from about 23,000 in September) and Temporary Protected Status visa revocations as downside risks.

Bank of America doesn’t expect the report to move December Fed pricing much. With the banks bunched at 75,000, the surprise is more likely to come from the unemployment rate and wages. 4.1% with 0.3% wage growth backs a December hike; 4.2% with 0.2% probably goes the other way.

tweets.text:
Not surprisingly given his "top forecaster" record with Bloomberg for the EU, @C_Barraud flagged eurozone producer prices coming in above 11.0% as “very likely” against a Bloomberg consensus of 10.6%. Eurostat printed 11.1%, up from an upwardly revised 8.3% in August and the first double-digit reading since February 2023.

While I wouldn't normally post on EU PPI, Christophe's focus on the print is for a reason.  First, the specifics:

▪️ Month-over-month: +2.5% after +2.0% in August
▪️ Energy: +30.8% year-over-year, up from 21.0% in August
▪️ Excluding energy: +3.5% year-over-year, +0.1% month-over-month

So, energy drives the headline, but the ECB needs to be watching that ex-energy number. At 3.5% year-over-year it’s the highest since May 2023, up from 1.4% in March. Historically, ex-energy producer prices have led consumer goods inflation by about seven months, with a 0.88 correlation since 2001.

So that would point to an acceleration in EU CPI at an awkward time for the ECB:

▪️ It has hiked twice this year to a 2.50% deposit rate, then held last week. Lagarde said she sees no “material risk of second-round effects at the moment.”
▪️ Euro area consumer core inflation held at 2.5% in October. That flat core was part of the ECB’s case for patience.
▪️ Markets price two to three more hikes over the next year, per Reuters, with the Bundesbank and Bank of Italy heads signaling December is likely.
▪️ France is the complication. The 10-year OAT touched about 5% on October 1, and OAT-Bund spreads hit a 15-year high on October 22. France is also under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure, which makes the ECB’s backstop harder to use. ABN AMRO pushed its hike calls back to December and March, partly because of the bond selloff.
▪️ Then there’s the leadership turnover. Lagarde leaves February 7, nine months early, likely in part so EU leaders can choose her successor before France’s April-May presidential election. Schnabel leaves January 3 for the IMF, and Lane’s term ends May 31. That’s half the Executive Board turning over in the next six months.

While the ECB has plenty of reasons to go slow, including French spreads, weak growth and a leadership handoff, the pipeline is concerning. On the historical relationship, today’s 3.5% points to goods inflation of about 1.5% by spring from 1.2% now. 

So the real risk is whether energy keeps pushing ex-energy prices higher from here. The cleanest comparison is 2008. An oil shock pushed energy producer prices to 23.9% that July, and ex-energy producer prices peaked at 4.0%, not far from today’s 3.5%. Yet core never moved, holding at 1.7%. 

The ECB famously hiked into it anyway and was cutting by October, then did the same in 2011. That history, plus French spreads and a leadership handoff, explains the reluctance now. Outside 2021–23 which had its own supply side dynamics, every 10 points of energy producer-price inflation has added only about 0.1 point to core a year later, which on history puts core near 2.7% next fall rather than breaking out. 

The catch is the starting point: core is 2.5% and services 3.3%, versus 1.7% and 2.6% in 2008. And 2008’s energy shock didn’t fade on its own; the financial crisis ended it. If energy is still compounding by January, when firms reset prices, the ECB will likely find itself forced to continue hiking irrespective of what's going on with French bond yields.

Apparently the Wednesday rally came too late to save the AAII survey as American Association of Individual Investors (AAII), a retail focused weekly investor survey, edged more bearish:

AAII Bulls (those who see higher stock prices in 6 months, blue line) fell to 34.1%, the least in six weeks, from 37.8% the prior week (still though above the 28.8% seven weeks ago, which was the least since September 2025), and falling back below the long-term historic average of 37.5% after a week above.

Bulls also remained below the level of the Bears (who see lower stock prices in 6 months, red line), as the Bears rose to 48.4%, the most in seven weeks, from 41.4% the prior week (still though below the 53.3% seven weeks ago, the highest since May 2025). That leaves Bulls above Bears just twice in the last 16 weeks. Bears also remain above the long-term average of 31.0% for a 38th straight week (and they’ve only been below it 9 weeks since Dec 12, 2024).

The Neutral camp (yellow line) dropped to 17.5%, the least in two weeks, from 20.7% (just above the 17.3% two weeks ago, which was the least since early April). It remains under the long-run average of 31.5% and has been over that only twice since July 2024.
